title: IndiGo Flight from Lucknow to Dammam Makes Emergency Landing in Ahmedabad After Bomb Note Found
excerpt: All 107 passengers and six crew on flight 6E97 were deplaned safely; nothing suspicious was found after searches by police, CISF, and bomb disposal squads.
body:
• IndiGo flight 6E97 from Lucknow to Dammam, Saudi Arabia, made an emergency landing at Ahmedabad airport on September 10 after a crew member found the word "bomb" written on a piece of tissue paper.
  • The aircraft landed around 5:55 pm with 107 passengers and six crew members; all were deplaned safely, according to police.
  • Police, CISF, fire teams, and bomb disposal squads searched the aircraft and found nothing suspicious; handwriting samples were collected from passengers for comparison.
  • This was Ahmedabad airport's second emergency landing of a flight in just 10 days, amid a continuing wave of hoax threats against Indian airlines.

The Incident

An IndiGo flight bound for Dammam in Saudi Arabia made an emergency landing in Ahmedabad on September 10 after a bomb threat note was discovered on board. The aircraft, operating as flight 6E97 from Lucknow, landed at Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel International Airport at around 5:55 pm.

"A crew member found 'bomb' written on a piece of paper on the flight, after which it made an emergency landing at Ahmedabad Airport. The flight was carrying 107 passengers and six crew members. They were made to disembark."

— A D Chavda, Airport police inspector, quoted by PTI

Airport police, fire teams, and bomb squad officials moved quickly. The local police and the Central Industrial Security Force searched the aircraft thoroughly and found nothing suspicious. Passengers were reportedly asked to write on tissue paper so their handwriting could be compared with the writing on the suspicious note — a standard investigative step to trace who planted it.

The incident marked Ahmedabad airport's second emergency landing within just 10 days, underlining how frequently Indian aviation is dealing with such scares.

Context & Background

Hoax bomb threats have plagued Indian airlines for over a year, arriving through social media posts, emails, and — as in this case — notes left inside aircraft. In one 24-hour stretch last October, security agencies received at least 10 threats across multiple airports, some reportedly originating from accounts based in London and other countries.

Every Indian airport operates a Bomb Threat Assessment Committee that evaluates the severity of each threat, but protocol leaves no room for discretion: aircraft are diverted, grounded, or evacuated; passengers are disembarked; and bomb squads, sniffer dogs, and police teams sweep the plane and baggage. Ahmedabad itself has seen a cluster of incidents — a Madinah-to-Hyderabad flight with over 180 people was diverted there last year after a mid-air threat, and a Kuwait-to-Delhi flight with 186 people on board made an emergency landing at the airport after a handwritten threat on tissue paper was found mid-flight.

The Lucknow-Dammam scare follows the same pattern: a tissue-paper note, maximum disruption, and ultimately nothing found.

Impact & Analysis

For the 107 passengers — many of them workers traveling to jobs in Saudi Arabia — the diversion meant hours of delay, security re-screening, and missed onward connections. IndiGo, which has borne a disproportionate share of these hoaxes, reiterated its standard position that passenger and crew safety remains paramount and that standard operating procedures were followed with the relevant authorities.

The economic cost of the hoax wave is significant: diverted aircraft burn fuel and crew hours, airports deploy emergency resources, and schedules cascade into delays across the network. Airlines and security agencies have pushed for stricter legal action against those behind the threats. Police have registered cases under provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita dealing with acts endangering human life, and suspended social media accounts used to post threats.

The handwriting-comparison step in the Ahmedabad case suggests investigators are treating the note as traceable evidence rather than an anonymous prank — a sign that enforcement is tightening.

Diaspora Angle

The Lucknow-Dammam route is heavily used by Indian migrant workers heading to jobs in the Gulf, for whom a missed connection or a lost day of work carries real financial cost. These travelers — often flying on tight budgets and tighter schedules — are the least able to absorb the disruption that hoax threats cause. Each emergency landing is a reminder that the price of these pranks falls hardest on working-class passengers.

What's Next

Investigators are working to identify who wrote the note, with handwriting samples collected from passengers. Officials have not yet confirmed the exact circumstances behind the incident, and the aircraft will remain subject to security holds until cleared. IndiGo has not announced when the flight will depart for Dammam. With the hoax-threat wave showing no sign of abating, aviation security experts expect the government's push for deterrent penalties — including no-fly listings and criminal prosecution — to intensify.
